source: Fugelsang & Dunbar (2005) Brain-based mechanisms underlying complex causal thinking
finding: People judged a causal drug theory partly by how plausible it was, not only by the data. Data that matched the theory were weighted more, so the same covariation counted for more under a plausible theory.
numbers: N=14 students, within-subject. Plausibility F(1,13)=5.2, eta2=.29. Covariation F(1,13)=81.37, eta2=.86. Interaction F(1,13)=10.48, eta2=.45: data effect 1.29 rating points under a plausible theory vs 0.57 under an implausible one.
limits: Small N. Rating scale 1-3. Artificial pill task, not real expert work.
agent_relevance: Prior plausibility changes how much a new observation moves the belief. The agent should record a prior plausibility and not let it silently discount data.

source: Fugelsang & Dunbar (2005) Brain-based mechanisms underlying complex causal thinking
finding: Brain scans split two ways. Data that fit a plausible theory recruited memory/learning areas. Data that clashed with a plausible theory recruited conflict-monitoring areas (dorsal anterior cingulate, left DLPFC, precuneus).
numbers: 14 participants, fMRI, threshold P=.001 uncorrected. Conflict network seen only for inconsistent data against a PLAUSIBLE theory, not against an implausible one.
limits: Uncorrected threshold, small N. Reverse inference from regions to process is weak.
agent_relevance: A clash is detected only when the held belief is strong. This matches our idea that a conflict signal should fire on failed checks against a confident rule, and be weak for low-confidence rules.

source: Fugelsang & Dunbar (2005) Brain-based mechanisms underlying complex causal thinking
finding: Authors read the conflict pattern as the brain treating inconsistent data as error, with attention reallocated away from it.
numbers: Same study. They link precuneus + DLPFC to reallocating attention and inhibiting the task-relevant processing of the unwelcome data.
limits: Interpretation, not tested directly. Authors cite Ahn et al. 1995: beliefs with a known mechanism are kept more firmly.
agent_relevance: Beliefs backed by a named mechanism are the hardest to dislodge. A rule with a stated mechanism needs a harder trigger than a bare pattern.

source: Trickett, Trafton & Schunn (2001) That's Odd! How Scientists Respond to Anomalous Data (CogSci)
finding: Working scientists noticed anomalies often and gave them more attention than expected results. This is the opposite of a simple confirmation-bias story.
numbers: 3 scientists, 2 domains. Astronomy session ~53 min, 649 on-task segments, 19 episodes; physics ~15 min, 176 segments, 9 episodes. At least 1/3 (astronomy) and nearly 1/2 (physics) of noticings were anomalous. Subsequent references per noticing: anomalies 7.6 (astronomy) and 3.0 (physics); anomalies got over 3x (astronomy) and over 2x (physics) the references of expected items; t(28)=2.33, p<.05.
quote: The results are in stark contrast to the findings of the confirmation bias literature.
limits: Tiny N (3 people, one session each). Scientists analysed their own data in a visual display. Short sessions give no view of long-term fixation.
agent_relevance: Real experts do attend to odd results. But attending is not the same as revising a frame.

source: Trickett, Trafton & Schunn (2001) That's Odd! (CogSci)
finding: After noticing an anomaly, scientists proposed a hypothesis and elaborated it using the data display, not their domain theory. None of the noticings were placed in global theoretical context.
numbers: Chi-square(1)=7.5 p<.05 for more hypotheses on anomalies; chi-square(1)=9.21 p<.01 for more placement in local (dataset) context. Astronomy: 4 of 5 anomaly hypotheses developed from the display; both hypotheses about expected items were theory-based.
limits: Counts are very small (5 and 2 hypotheses). Authors flag no theory-based elaboration at all, which may reflect the visual-analysis task.
agent_relevance: Resolution of a surprise happened by comparing with other data, which a program can do (compare to other runs, other examples) without asking the model for its opinion.

source: Trickett, Trafton & Schunn (2009) How do scientists respond to anomalies? (Cognitive Science)
finding: Search-result summary only (PDF not retrievable). Study 1: physicists and meteorologists in basic vs applied work; basic scientists resolved anomalies by mental simulation, applied scientists by mentally manipulating the image. Study 2: novice meteorologists used comparison where experts did not.
numbers: Not extracted. Two in vivo studies.
limits: Unopened; read the PDF before use.
agent_relevance: Strategy for resolving an anomaly depends on goal and expertise, so one fixed resolution move is wrong.

source: Kan, Pizzonia, Drummey & Mikkelsen (2021) Exploring factors that mitigate the continued influence of misinformation
finding: Exp 1A: a correction that names the false claim AND offers an alternative cause cut references to the false claim to near zero. A vague correction with no alternative did nothing.
numbers: 252 students tested, 248 usable. Misinformation score (max 6): direct+alternative 0.20, indirect+alternative 0.22, direct no alternative 0.81, indirect no alternative 2.78. Interaction F(1,169)=26.19, partial eta2=.13. Indirect no-alternative was statistically equivalent to no correction at all (TOST p=.011).
limits: One story (minibus accident), student sample, immediate test. Equivalence tests said alternative corrections did not fully reach the never-misinformed baseline in Exp 1A. Author list from memory; check.
agent_relevance: Telling the model 'that was wrong' is nearly useless. The retraction must name the wrong claim and supply a replacement.

source: Kan et al. (2021)
finding: Elimination of the continued influence effect is rare. The paper cites the situation-model view: people prefer a complete but flawed model over one with a gap, and discredited items stay active in memory.
numbers: Across 3 studies and 2 outcome measures alternative provision always reduced the effect; combined alternative + direct targeting eliminated it only under some conditions.
limits: Mechanism accounts (gap-filling vs residual activation) are not separated by this paper.
agent_relevance: Supports a rule: a revision step must always produce a candidate replacement frame, not only delete the old one.

source: Chan, Jones, Hall Jamieson & Albarracin (2017) Debunking: a meta-analysis of messages countering misinformation (Psychological Science)
finding: Debunking works but does not erase the belief. Persistence of misinformation after a correction is still a medium-to-large effect.
numbers: k=52 samples, N=6,878 (8 reports, 20 experiments). Misinformation effect d=2.41-3.08; debunking effect d=1.14-1.33; persistence after debunking d=0.75-1.06. Mostly student samples, mean age 20, 72% female.
limits: Mostly lab text vignettes. Persistence measured as difference from a no-misinformation group, so it is a floor estimate of lingering influence.
agent_relevance: A single retraction leaves a sizeable residue. Expect residue in the model's later steps and design checks that look for it.

source: Chan et al. (2017)
finding: Moderators: persistence was stronger and debunking weaker when people generated their own reasons supporting the misinformation. Detailed debunking messages improved debunking but also raised persistence.
numbers: Directions only from abstract: generating support reasons raises persistence; detail correlates positively with both debunking and persistence (exact moderator coefficients not recorded).
limits: Correlational moderators, not randomised. Authors call the detail result surprising.
agent_relevance: If the model has already written reasons for a rule, those reasons act as a shield. Drop or quarantine them before reframing.

source: Wood & Porter (2019) The Elusive Backfire Effect (Political Behavior)
finding: Large failed replication of the backfire effect. Corrections did not make people hold the false belief more strongly on any issue tested.
numbers: 5 experiments, more than 10,100 subjects, 52 issues. No correction triggered backfire. The original Nyhan & Reifler (2010) found backfire on 2 high-salience issues (Iraq WMD, tax cuts) and none on stem cells.
limits: Short-term one-shot survey corrections. Ideology still shaped how much people updated. Does not show corrections work fully.
agent_relevance: Do not build the agent on the claim that showing contrary evidence entrenches a belief. The measured risk is ignoring or under-weighting, not reversal.

source: Wood & Porter (2019)
finding: Two competing mechanisms were tested: weak vague corrections vs forceful ones provoking counter-arguing. Neither produced backfire.
numbers: Same 5 studies. Section 'Does Counterargument Explain Our Pattern of Findings?' tests both on all corrections.
limits: Counter-arguing was only inferred from correction style, not measured.
agent_relevance: Rival theories (counter-arguing) have little support in this setting; keep guardrails simple.

source: Walter & Tukachinsky (2020) A meta-analytic examination of the continued influence of misinformation (Communication Research)
finding: Per search summary: corrections generally do not fully erase misinformation. Corrections worked better when coherent, matched worldview and came from the misinformation's source. Worse when the source was credible, when misinformation was repeated, or when time passed.
numbers: k=32 studies, N=6,527, r=-.05 p=.045 for the overall effect per search summary only.
limits: Unopened (PDF download returned HTML). Numbers from search snippet; verify.
agent_relevance: Repetition and delay make retraction less effective: argue for correcting early, before an assumption is repeated across turns.

source: Lord, Lepper & Preston (1984) Considering the opposite (JPSP)
finding: Telling people to consider the opposite reduced biased assimilation more than telling them to be fair and unbiased.
numbers: Two experiments per search summary; effect sizes not retrieved.
limits: Unopened. No direct replication found in one search. Old, student samples.
agent_relevance: Supports a 'generate the contrary case' move, and weakens a plain 'be objective' instruction.

source: Xie et al. (2024) Adaptive Chameleon or Stubborn Sloth (ICLR)
finding: When the only evidence contradicts what the model knows and is coherent, LLMs mostly accept it. When supportive and contradicting evidence are both present, they cling to their own prior (confirmation bias).
numbers: Models include ChatGPT, GPT-4, PaLM2, Llama2-7B/70B, Vicuna. Multi-source memorization ratio is significantly higher than single-source, especially GPT-4. GPT-4 reaches an 80% memorization ratio on the most popular questions.
limits: Counter-evidence is generated by ChatGPT, so it may be unusually fluent. Closed-book facts, not reasoning traces.
agent_relevance: In our schema the model's own earlier attempt acts like parametric memory. Contrary evidence mixed with supporting items will be under-weighted. Show contrary evidence on its own first.

source: Xie et al. (2024)
finding: Confirmation bias grows with how much memory-supporting evidence is present, even at fixed proportion, and evidence order changes answers a lot for most models.
numbers: Table 6: GPT-4 and Vicuna-33B still cling to memory even when 2 of 3 items support the counter answer (ratio 1/3). Order sensitivity above 5% for all but GPT-4; PaLM2 and Llama2-7B above 30%. Llama2-7B log-prob of memory answer >=95% in 96.3% of sampled multi-source cases.
limits: Older models. Newer reasoning models not tested.
agent_relevance: Program must randomise or control evidence order and count items, not leave that to the model.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR)
finding: Without an external signal, asking a model to review and fix its answer lowers accuracy. Earlier gains came from using the true label to decide when to stop.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5 75.9 -> 75.1 -> 74.7; GPT-4 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0. CommonSenseQA GPT-3.5 75.8 -> 38.1 -> 41.8; GPT-4 82.0 -> 79.5 -> 80.0. HotpotQA GPT-3.5 26.0 -> 25.0 -> 25.0; GPT-4 49.0 -> 49.0 -> 43.0 (round 0, 1, 2). GPT-3.5 kept its GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time and, when it changed, more often went right-to-wrong.
limits: 2023-era models; GPT-4 sampled to 200 questions (100 HotpotQA). Does not cover tasks with real tool feedback.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G1 and G2: no self-triggered doubt, revise only from real output.

source: Huang et al. (2024)
finding: Multi-agent debate was no better than self-consistency at equal response count, and a prompt that says the answer might be wrong hurts.
numbers: Paper reports debate no better than self-consistency at matched number of responses; default feedback prompt 'Assume that this answer could be either correct or incorrect...' reduced accuracy in all settings tested.
limits: Exact debate table values not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Do not spend budget on critique rounds without a check.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: Models fix early assumptions and then do not recover when later information corrects them. This is garden-path fixation in LLMs.
numbers: 15 LLMs, 6 tasks, 600 instructions, N=10 runs each, over 200,000 conversations. Average drop 39% from single-turn to sharded multi-turn. Aptitude -15 to -16%, unreliability +112%. Best-to-worst run gap about 50 points.
quote: when LLMs take a wrong turn in a conversation, they get lost and do not recover
limits: Synthetic sharded instructions; user simulator is an LLM. Fixation inferred from behaviour (premature answers, reliance on prior attempts).
agent_relevance: The main damage is variance, not average skill: a wrong early frame leaves the run stuck. Restart from the full restated problem rather than patching.

source: Laban et al. (2025)
finding: Remedies tried: restating all information. Lower temperature and extra thinking did not fix it.
numbers: RECAP (restate at end) and SNOWBALL (restate every turn) with GPT-4o and 4o-mini: SNOWBALL recovers only 15-20% of the loss. Temperature 0 for both sides still leaves unreliability near 30% for GPT-4o. Reasoning models o3 and DeepSeek-R1 degrade like others; their replies are on average 33% longer, and longer replies carry more assumptions.
limits: Only two models in the restatement tests. RECAP uses knowledge of the last turn, so it is unrealistic.
agent_relevance: Test-time compute alone does not break fixation. A program-led fresh restart with a clean statement is the stronger move.

source: Laban et al. (2025)
finding: Fixation shows up in the answers: correct programs reached in multi-turn runs are longer, hinting the early wrong frame was patched, not replaced.
numbers: Code: correct solutions 850 characters vs 668 in single-turn (27% longer). SQL: 129 vs 113 characters (14% longer).
limits: Only for solutions that ended fully correct.
agent_relevance: Patching bloat is a measurable sign of an unreplaced frame; a length check could be a cheap anomaly signal to test on our logs.

source: Samadarshi et al. (2024) LLMs are Fixated by Red Herrings (Only Connect Wall)
finding: On a puzzle built with deliberate red herrings, LLMs fall far below humans, and performance rises when red herrings are removed. The authors link this to the human fixation and Einstellung effects.
numbers: Human connection-naming score about 80%; best GPT-4 10-shot score 41-45% F1. More in-context examples (1 to 10) did not help. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 improved significantly on OCW-Randomized and OCW-WordNet, which have fewer red herrings (numbers in the paper's Table 5, not recorded). Author list from memory; check.
limits: Quiz-show data, UK-centric, possible leakage. Human-vs-model comparison is approximate. Not a causal test of the retrieval mechanism.
agent_relevance: A decoy that fits two groups traps models. When two candidate frames both fit, the program should keep both open instead of letting the model pick one.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Limitations of LLMs in clinical problem-solving arising from inflexible reasoning (M-ARC)
finding: Questions built to trigger the Einstellung effect in medicine: LLMs score below physicians and are overconfident.
numbers: 100 questions. Physicians averaged 66% (5 physicians, SE 5.3 points). Best models Gemini-1.5-Pro 50% and o1 48%; several near or below 20%. Brier scores show overconfidence.
limits: Only 100 hand-made items, only 5 physicians (who also fall for the effect). Scenarios are unusual.
agent_relevance: Models match the familiar pattern even when a small detail breaks it. Confidence is not a usable anomaly signal.

source: Kenaston et al. (2025) Cognitive bias in LLM reasoning compromises interpretation of clinical oncology notes
finding: GPT-4 oncology-note errors were mostly reasoning failures, with confirmation bias and anchoring over-represented in harmful recommendations.
numbers: Taxonomy built on 600 responses from 40 notes; applied to 822 responses from 24 prostate notes. Error rate 23.1% (+-0.8), inter-rater 0.85, reasoning failures 85.4% of errors. Automated evaluators detected an error but could not classify subtype reliably.
limits: Single model (GPT-4). Bias labels are applied by authors to text, a mapping not a proven mechanism.
agent_relevance: Model-based bias labelling is unreliable; detect fixation with counts and checks, not with a judge naming the bias.

source: Xu et al. (2024) Knowledge Conflicts for LLMs: A Survey
finding: Survey sorts conflicts into context-memory, inter-context and intra-memory, and lists fixes by goal: stay faithful to context or stay faithful to memory.
numbers: Fixes named: opinion-based prompts and counterfactual demonstrations (Zhou 2023), context-aware decoding (Shi 2023), vigilant prompting against misinformation (Pan 2023). Effect sizes not recorded.
limits: Survey; fixes are mostly short-task QA and not shown to hold in long reasoning runs.
agent_relevance: Two goals pull opposite ways. Our agent must pick one by rule: trust a verified check over memory, but not unverified context over a verified result.

source: Saposnik et al. (2016) Cognitive biases associated with medical decisions: a systematic review (BMC Med Inform Decis Mak)
finding: Across physician studies, anchoring, overconfidence and availability bias were linked to wrong diagnoses in a large share of vignettes.
numbers: 114 papers screened, 20 studies, 6,810 physicians (median 180). Anchoring, overconfidence, information and availability biases tied to diagnostic inaccuracy in 36.5 to 77% of case scenarios. 14 of 20 studies used narrative vignettes; only 6 used real-life measures. Only 2 studies looked at patient outcomes and one found a link.
limits: Mostly vignettes. Observational. Heterogeneous measures so no pooled effect size.
agent_relevance: Fixation in experts is common but evidence of harm in practice is thin; do not oversell it.

source: Rudolph (conference abstract) Diagnostic failure modes in simulated OR crisis
finding: Per search summary: in a high-fidelity OR crisis simulation, residents reached the correct diagnosis only about 23% of the time. Failures were split into few differentials (5%), failure to abandon an early diagnosis (28%), and moving between diagnoses without testing them (44%).
numbers: Numbers from a search snippet of a conference abstract; N not seen.
limits: Unopened. Needs primary paper.
agent_relevance: Important rival: the bigger failure is not fixation but hopping between untested ideas, so a reframe must be a tested move, not a switch.

source: Schwid & O'Donnell (1992) Anesthesiologists' management of simulated critical incidents (Anesthesiology)
finding: Per search summary: with 30 anesthesiologists (10 residents, 10 faculty, 10 private practitioners), fixation errors, meaning failure to revise a plan despite inconsistent cues, occurred in 63% of subjects.
numbers: 63% of 30 per search summary; authorship attribution unverified.
limits: Unopened (PubMed page blocked). Old simulator study, small N. Author names not confirmed.
agent_relevance: Fixation seen in experts as well as trainees; no expertise immunity.

source: Chinn & Brewer (1993/1998) taxonomy of responses to anomalous data
finding: Seven responses: ignore, reject, exclude from theory domain, hold in abeyance, reinterpret, peripheral change, theory change. Only the last accepts the data. Per search summary, six of seven protect the theory.
numbers: No frequencies retrieved for the 1998 empirical test (JRST 35:623-654).
limits: Unopened; full text blocked in this session (Ideals returned 403). Taxonomy is coded by hand and categories may overlap.
agent_relevance: Gives codable categories for our logs: a run that discards a failed check as noise equals 'reject'.

source: Mamede et al. (2010) Effect of availability bias and reflective reasoning on diagnostic accuracy (JAMA)
finding: Per search summary: structured reflection improved diagnosis of cases similar to those that caused availability bias.
numbers: N=36 residents. Score difference 2.03 (95% CI 1.49-2.57) for second-year and 2.31 (1.89-2.73) for first-year residents, P=.006. Not standardised effect sizes.
limits: Unopened. Small N, one site.
agent_relevance: Doubt works when structured and cued by a case feature, not as free reflection (see G1).

source: Gaba & DeAnda (1990) CASE simulator incidents
finding: Per search summary: 19 simulations, 132 unplanned incidents, 27% critical; fixation about 20% of incidents.
numbers: Search snippet only.
limits: Unopened; the snippet source does not clearly attribute these figures.
agent_relevance: Low-weight support only.
